clinicalPearls: Acute, self-limited systemic viral illness typically characterized by parotitis or other salivary gland swelling; suspect in any patient with parotitis or mumps complications regardless of age, vaccination status, or travel history (p.1646).

Parotitis is generally bilateral but may not be synchronous on both sides; unilateral involvement occurs in about one-third of cases, with tenderness and obliteration of the space between the earlobe and angle of the mandible (p.1647).

Parotitis is often preceded by a several-day prodrome of low-grade fever, malaise, myalgia, headache, and anorexia; it typically lasts ~5 days (range 3-7) with most cases resolving within 10 days (p.1647).
Infection is asymptomatic in ~20% of unvaccinated patients; it can also present as nonspecific respiratory symptoms (p.1647).
Fully vaccinated persons can still contract mumps, but are at lower risk for mumps and for mumps complications (p.1647).

Buccal swabs are the best specimens for virus detection; the parotid gland should be massaged for 30 s before collection, and specimens collected as close to parotitis onset as possible (maximal shedding within 5 days of symptom onset) (p.1649).
Complications can occur in the absence of parotitis and are more common in adults than children and in males than females (largely due to orchitis) (p.1648).
harrison.pathophysiology: Caused by mumps virus, a single-stranded negative-sense enveloped RNA paramyxovirus (Rubulavirus genus, Paramyxoviridae); there is only one serotype (p.1646). Humans are the only known natural reservoir; transmission is via direct contact with respiratory droplets or saliva of an infected person. Incubation averages 16-18 days (range 12-25). A person is most infectious from 2 days before until 5 days after onset of parotitis (virus detected in saliva as early as 7 days before to as late as 9 days after onset) (p.1647). Primary replication likely occurs in the nasal/upper respiratory mucosal epithelium, with spread to regional lymph nodes and infection of mononuclear cells facilitating viremia lasting ~3-5 days. Viremia produces acute inflammatory reactions most commonly in the salivary glands (parotitis) and testes (orchitis), with dissemination also to kidneys, CNS, pancreas, heart, ovaries, mammary glands, cochlear perilymph, and (in pregnancy) the fetus. Mumps encephalitis in many cases appears to be a para- or postinfectious demyelinating process rather than direct viral cytotoxicity, though rare primary encephalitis with viral isolation from brain tissue does occur (p.1647-1648).
additionalDifferentials: Influenza A H3N2 (can increase parotitis cases)
Laundry starch ingestion / malnutrition / cirrhosis and some drug treatments
Salivary duct obstruction, cysts, or tumors (cause of unilateral parotitis)
Bacterial prostatic/urinary tract infection, chlamydia, gonorrhea, and viral orchitis (coxsackievirus, varicella, echovirus, CMV)
infectionMimics: Enteroviral aseptic meningitis (clinically indistinguishable from mumps meningitis)
nonInfectiousMimics: Salivary ductal obstruction, cysts, or tumors
additionalInvestigations: RT-PCR (preferred virologic confirmation) on blood, saliva, urine, or CSF; buccal swab is the best specimen
Mumps-specific IgM serology (note: often undetectable, transient, or delayed in vaccinated patients, and can give false positives from cross-reactions)
Paired acute- and convalescent-phase IgG for a fourfold rise (IgG testing generally not recommended, as titers may already be elevated in vaccinated/previously infected patients)
Serum amylase and lipase (both elevated suggests pancreatitis in addition to parotitis)
redFlags: Orchitis (most common complication; up to 30% of unvaccinated and 6% of vaccinated postpubertal males) with possible testicular atrophy and temporary subfertility
Aseptic meningitis (up to 10% of unvaccinated, <=1% of vaccinated patients)
Encephalitis (<=1% of patients; high fever, altered consciousness, seizures, focal neurologic signs; mortality ~1.5%)
Sensorineural hearing loss / deafness (usually sudden, unilateral, transient; bilateral and permanent loss are rare)
Supraglottic edema (rare, life-threatening) from obstructed lymphatic drainage
Other CNS complications: cerebellar ataxia, facial palsy, transverse myelitis, hydrocephalus, Guillain-Barre syndrome, flaccid paralysis
Myocarditis and endocardial fibroelastosis (rare but potentially severe)
harrison.prognosis: Generally a benign, self-resolving illness; death due to mumps is exceedingly rare (p.1648). Aseptic meningitis is self-limited without significant risk of death or long-term sequelae. Encephalitis carries a mortality of ~1.5%, may leave permanent sequelae, and has poorer outcomes in adults than children. Orchitis can cause testicular atrophy in ~30-50% of affected testicles and temporary sterility/subfertility, but no studies have assessed the risk of permanent infertility. Mumps-related hearing loss is usually transient; bilateral permanent loss is rare. Mumps in pregnancy is generally benign and no more severe than in non-pregnant women, and evidence for an association with increased spontaneous abortion or fetal death is inconclusive (p.1648).
pitfalls: A negative virologic or serologic result does NOT rule out mumps in a person with clinical signs, especially in vaccinated patients (p.1649).
Failure to detect mumps IgM is very common in vaccinated patients (IgM response often undetectable, transient, or delayed); IgM can also yield false positives from cross-reactions (p.1649).
Presence of parotitis, orchitis, or oophoritis supports a mumps diagnosis but their absence does NOT exclude it; complications can occur without parotitis (p.1648).

A positive IgG titer indicates only prior exposure (vaccination or natural infection) and does NOT predict protection; IgG titers should NOT be used to infer immunity in close contacts since they may instead reflect acute infection (p.1649).
Elevated serum amylase can arise from parotitis OR pancreatitis; lipase is needed to distinguish (p.1648).
Mumps reinfection and recurrent infection can occur and may be more common than previously thought (p.1648).

MMR vaccine has NOT been shown to prevent illness or alter severity in persons already infected and is NOT recommended as postexposure prophylaxis; mumps immune globulin is also NOT recommended for postexposure prophylaxis or treatment (p.1649).
harrison.severityClassification: No formal severity classification in the source. Spectrum ranges from asymptomatic infection (~20% of unvaccinated) through classic self-limited parotitis to complicated disease (orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, hearing loss, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis); subclinical CNS involvement (CSF pleocytosis) occurs in up to 55% of patients.
management: No specific antiviral therapy; management is supportive with analgesia, antipyretics, hydration and rest during the self-limiting illness
Local supportive measures for parotitis, including analgesia and avoidance of acidic foods that stimulate painful salivary secretion
Supportive care for orchitis with scrotal support and anti-inflammatory agents, and monitoring for pancreatitis, oophoritis and mastitis
Assess and manage complications such as aseptic meningitis and encephalitis with supportive care and hospital admission where indicated
Isolate the patient with droplet precautions for the infectious period to limit transmission
Notify public health authorities and arrange post-exposure MMR vaccination of susceptible contacts, since prevention rests on immunisation
